Jacques walks through each mistake with enough specificity that you'll recognize your own habits. Practical and unpadded at under 26 minutes.

themes.name: Secrets, Codes & Fog of War
themes.tagline: From medieval tower conspiracies to WWII torpedo runs — history at its most gripping and unresolved.

items.title: What Happened To The Princes In The Tower?
items.description:
Medieval historian Eleanor Janega debates one of history's biggest mysteries of all time. What happened to the Princes in the Tower?

In 1483, young Edward V and his brother Richard were awaiting Edward's coronation. But next thing we know, they vanished, and their uncle Richard III has taken the throne. So what happened?

Eleanor Janega guides Anthony through this episode, with a special guest appearance by Eleanor's 'Gone Medieval' co-host Matt Lewis! 'Gone Medieval' is History Hit's medieval
items.why_watch: Medieval historian Eleanor Janega doesn't just rehearse the usual Richard III suspicion — she actually debates the evidence, weighing competing theories with academic rigor in a conversational format. At an hour, it's a genuine deep dive rather than a surface retelling of one of history's most enduring cold cases.

If you've seen the film but wondered how it really worked, this fills that gap precisely.

items.why_watch: In early 1942, when American war news was relentlessly grim, a small squadron of fast attack boats led by Lieutenant John Bulkeley became a rare source of genuine heroism — including evacuating MacArthur from the Philippines. History Guy tells the story with his usual restraint and affection for the genuinely forgotten, and it's over in under 17 minutes.

items.title: How Many Neutrons Can You Stack Before Reality Breaks?
items.description:
Note: At 27:15–27:35, there's a segment with flashing lights (pulsar simulation). Just a heads-up for anyone who might be sensitive to that.

You can help support this channel via the Physics Explained Patreon:

What happens if you keep adding neutrons—forever? Is there a limit? And what does quantum mechanics and relativity have to do with it?

This video explores the surprising physics of nuclear forces, quantum mechanics, and gravity to find out. We us
items.why_watch: This video uses the deceptively simple question of "what if you kept adding neutrons?" to walk you through neutron stars, the Pauli exclusion principle, and the point where quantum mechanics and general relativity collide catastrophically. The 1.7 million views are earned — it builds genuine understanding rather than just awe.

Chapters:
00:00 Intro

04:15 How to validate?

items.why_watch: The central insight here — that everything moves through spacetime at exactly the speed of light, trading spatial speed for time speed — reframes time dilation and length contraction as geometry rather than paradox. FloatHeadPhysics builds the idea carefully from a 2D analogy first, so the leap to four-dimensional spacetime feels natural rather than hand-wavy.

items.title: Newton vs. Mach: The Bucket Experiment
items.description:
What is the ultimate nature of motion? Two influential physicists famously debated this question, invoking a bucket-and-water thought experiment to do so -- but they arrived at starkly different conclusions. Can we determine which one of them was right? Join us on a journey that spans centuries of metaphysical thought, books worth of controversial literature, and twenty-minutes of bad attempts at animating water spinning in a bucket.

Contents:

00:00 - Intro
01:05 - Newton's Absolutes
04:15 - T
items.why_watch: Newton's rotating bucket thought experiment seems straightforward until Mach points out that it quietly assumes the entire universe is the reference frame — a challenge that Einstein took seriously enough to shape general relativity. Dialect unpacks this centuries-long disagreement with genuine philosophical precision, making it one of the more intellectually satisfying 21-minute detours in physics history.

items.why_watch: Most differential amplifier explanations jump straight to formulas; this one starts with a qualitative walkthrough of why the circuit rejects common-mode signals before the math appears, which makes the equations feel earned rather than imposed. Useful whether you're working with MOSFETs or BJTs, since the video treats their shared working principle as the actual lesson.

morning_soundtrack.title: Rhiannon Giddens' banjo connects her to her ancestors: 'The spirits come through'
morning_soundtrack.snippet: A self-described "folkie to the bone," Giddens sings and plays banjo and fiddle in this interview. Her latest album, Hope Is the Thing with Feathers , takes its name from an Emily Dickinson poem.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like sitting on a porch at dusk while the past reaches through the floorboards to hold your hand.

morning_soundtrack.title: Claire Cronin – “Before The End Of Time”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The LA-based writer and musician Claire Cronin's work is generally based around ideas of folk horror and spiritual dread. Her 2020 book Blue Light Of The Screen is about her obsession with horror movies, which also tends to come through in her music. But Cronin's latest song, is a gorgeous lullaby about how she'll miss the world once it ends.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A tender goodbye letter to existence, hummed softly before the lights go out for good.

morning_soundtrack.title: Lydia Loveless Announces New EP Accolades, Shares New Version Of Title Track
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Columbus country-rocker Lydia Loveless released their last album Nothing's Gonna Stand In My Way Again in 2023. Last year Loveless shared a series of one-off writing-challenge tracks on Bandcamp, including a very good song called " Accolades ." They've since taken down most of those Bandcamp tracks, "Accolades" included. Next month, Loveless will release a brand new EP that's called Accolades , and it's lead single is a brand-new version of the title track.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Bar-closing energy with a bruised heart and just enough swagger to drive home anyway.

morning_soundtrack.title: FOUNDERS KEEPERS: Claire Kelly Leads an Impressive Batch of New Music from Americana Women
morning_soundtrack.snippet: You never know where you’ll find an artist who rocks your world. Last summer, a trip to the upper Midwest included the Mile of Music Fest in Appleton, Wis., where I saw several sets by Nashville singer-songwriter Claire Kelly and her red-hot backing band, which blew
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The electric jolt of stumbling onto a great live act in a town you'd never planned to stop in.

morning_soundtrack.title: Rainy Day Parade: The Sad/Happy Story of Jill Sobule
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Editor's Note : David Hajdu has been awarded one of two No Depression Reporting Fellowships to write four in-depth features on a topic deeply impacting roots music today. His begins today with a multi-perspective profile of singer-songwriter Jill Sobule — part biography, part
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Crying and laughing at the same time in a kitchen that smells like coffee and old mail.

morning_soundtrack.title: Maddy Prior & June Tabor’s Silly Sisters at 50
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Maddy Prior and June Tabor’s Silly Sisters is a magical hinge album, a meeting of two transcendent voices and a jolly band of British folk masters. Recorded in 1976 but somehow outside of time, its ancient songs, close harmonies, and loose, luminous performances summon something older than the British folk revival itself. Fifty years on, it remains a timeless gem hiding in plain sight: raw, sophisticated, mysterious, and still not quite given its due.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like finding a door in your house you never noticed before, and hearing something ancient breathing softly on the other side.

morning_soundtrack.title: Dirty Honey Announce New Album, Unveil Singles “Lights Out” and “Butterfly”: Stream
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The album Catch My Butterfly will be released on January 15th. Dirty Honey Announce New Album, Unveil Singles “Lights Out” and “Butterfly”: Stream Spencer Kaufman
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Windows-down, volume-up rock that tastes like gasoline and lip gloss on a Friday night.

morning_soundtrack.title: Why Deadhead Culture Is a Pure Strain of American Noir
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Yes, Deadheads came for the music, but also for the possibility of a life outside the bounds of straight society; something vaguely criminal and very American noir.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Midnight on the highway with a trunk full of mysteries and no particular reason to go home.

morning_soundtrack.title: Rock Music Returns to Outside Lands 2026
morning_soundtrack.snippet: An exhilarating Friday featuring Wet Leg, Sierra Ferrell, Geese, Turnstile and Charli XCX brings rock back to San Francisco's Outside Lands Festival in a big way.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The bristling, crowd-surge feeling of a festival day that starts at noon and somehow never peaks too early.

global_silver_linings.title: New AI Model Can Detect Heart Disease Markers in Simple Electrocardiogram Readings–a Breakthrough
global_silver_linings.snippet: Artificial intelligence has brought about a revolution in medical screening practices, with the technology able to make detections across hundreds of scans in seconds which can be forwarded to trained pairs of human eyes. Now from the UK comes another example in the form of heart disease diagnostics. Trained on millions of patients, a new […]
global_silver_linings.reason: A new AI tool that can spot heart disease markers from a routine ECG means dangerous conditions could be caught far earlier, with equipment already found in most clinics. This kind of quiet, practical innovation has the potential to save countless lives without adding complexity or cost.

global_silver_linings.title: The race to get more young people in the UK into work, education or training
global_silver_linings.snippet: The UK has one of the highest NEET rates for young adults in Europe. New figures offer some encouragement
global_silver_linings.reason: Communities across the UK are finding creative, human-centred ways to connect young people with meaningful opportunities in work, education, and training. Every young person brought into that fold represents not just a life changed, but a future strengthened.

global_silver_linings.title: 12 photos of women before and after an orgasm shines a new light on women’s sexual wellness
global_silver_linings.snippet: "We hope that everyone viewing this project will feel more confident about their bodies and sexuality."
global_silver_linings.reason: Open, honest conversations about women's sexual wellness are slowly shedding stigma and helping people feel seen in their own experiences. Greater awareness and normalisation in this space is a genuine step toward better health and self-understanding for many.

global_silver_linings.title: Why Great Plains Ranchers Are Setting Fire to Their Own Land
global_silver_linings.snippet: Smoke hangs thick over southern Oklahoma’s Arbuckle Mountains as flames lick through prairie grass toward a stand of eastern red cedar trees. To many, the scene would look like a disaster in the making. But to father-son ranchers Chuck and Seth Coffey, the fire is a blessing — it’s the...
global_silver_linings.reason: Great Plains ranchers are reviving the ancient practice of controlled burning to restore native grasslands, bringing back the biodiversity that industrial farming had quietly erased. It's a heartening example of land stewards working with nature rather than against it.

global_silver_linings.title: How revisiting old memories can build real self-esteem
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Think about a memory that still makes you wince. Maybe it is the time you said something embarrassing in front of people you wanted to impress, or the moment you felt out of place while everyone around you seemed completely at ease. Most of us carry a few of […] The post How revisiting old memories can build real self-esteem first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Research suggests that thoughtfully revisiting our own past — including the hard parts — can help us build a more grounded and honest sense of self-worth. It's a reminder that real confidence doesn't come from forgetting where we've been, but from making peace with it.

discovery_articles.title: Old Route 5 Stone Wall in Nova Scotia
discovery_articles.snippet: This is a hidden gem in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia where a waterfall flows through an old stone wall, and cascades over mossy rocks in a steep, mossy canyon surrounded by birch trees. The waterfall and two other creeks converge in this canyon, before disappearing through a large culvert at the bottom. It's worth it to visit in the rain, when more water is running - and the rain just adds to the ambience.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A waterfall threading through a centuries-old stone wall, then vanishing into the earth through a culvert below — Cape Breton has somehow turned infrastructure into something genuinely haunting. Best appreciated, Fern suspects, in a light drizzle with no one else around.

discovery_articles.title: Puerta del Hospital de la Latina in Madrid, Spain
discovery_articles.snippet: There is something delightfully disorienting about stumbling across a 500-year-old Gothic doorway in the grounds of Madrid’s School of Architecture. Surrounded by modern university buildings and the comings and goings of students, the ornate stone portal looks as though it has taken a wrong turn somewhere in the city. In fact, it has—but quite a long time ago.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: This ornate Gothic doorway didn't always belong to a School of Architecture — it was relocated from a demolished 16th-century hospital, and has been quietly confusing passersby ever since. There's something almost poetic about a relic of mercy standing amid blueprints for the future.

discovery_articles.title: Roman Baths of Slovenia (Rimski Terma) in Slovenia
discovery_articles.snippet: In a valley surrounded by forested mountains is a mineral spring and baths in use since the Roman Empire. The baths were frequented by soldiers and royalty who wanted to take advantage of its purported healing properties. The land around the baths feature historical walking paths lined with trees donated to the area by high society visitors such by Victoria of Prussia who gifted a giant sequoia.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Roman soldiers soaked in these same mineral waters nearly two millennia ago, and somewhere nearby a giant sequoia planted by a Prussian princess is still quietly growing. History here isn't behind glass — it's rooted in the ground.

discovery_articles.title: Henry VIII Relied on This Courtier to Enforce His Orders During the English Reformation. Behind the Scenes, the Tudor Politician Defied His King by Secretly Saving a Catholic Text
discovery_articles.snippet: A newly discovered fragment suggests that John Gage preserved a 15th-century religious manuscript, keeping it "safe when he was meant to destroy books precisely like this one"
discovery_articles.ferns_note: John Gage spent his career as Henry VIII's loyal enforcer during the book-burning fury of the Reformation — all while secretly slipping a Catholic manuscript out of harm's way. The double life of a dutiful destroyer who couldn't quite bring himself to destroy.

discovery_articles.title: The Brain Shrinks as We Age and During Major Transitions. But Surprisingly, It Seems to Take a Break From Rewiring During Menopause
discovery_articles.snippet: Puberty, pregnancy and menopause are the three major hormonal transitions for the female brain. Researchers already knew that during the first two, the organ fine-tunes itself in response to hormonal shifts, but they haven't been sure about the third
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The brain apparently hits pause during menopause — unlike the intense rewiring it undergoes in puberty and pregnancy — which researchers find genuinely surprising rather than expected. It raises the quiet question of what, exactly, the brain is waiting for.

discovery_articles.title: Archaeologists Are Reconstructing the Invisible Technologies of the Stone Age, From Rope to Thread and Twine
discovery_articles.snippet: Largely missing from the archaeological record, fiber innovations played a huge role in the lives of early humans. Researchers are weaving together new insights from the traces they left behind
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Stone tools survive millennia; the ropes and nets that made them useful simply rot away, leaving us with a lopsided picture of early human ingenuity. Archaeologists are now reading the ghost impressions of fiber in clay and sediment to recover what time erased.

discovery_articles.title: An Armadillo Found in Ohio Is the Latest Surprise in the Armored Animals' Expansion North. Where Are They Now, and What's Driving Their Movement?
discovery_articles.snippet: Typically spotted in the South and Southeast, the creatures have been reaching increasingly distant states like North Carolina, Virginia and Illinois as winters become milder
discovery_articles.ferns_note: An armadillo turning up in Ohio is less a quirky headline and more a quiet dispatch from a warming continent — the armored little travelers are essentially mapping climate change one surprising sighting at a time. They've been moving north for decades; we're only just noticing.

discovery_articles.title: First radio waves seen from an exoplanet hint at otherworldly auroras
discovery_articles.snippet: The gas giant Beta Pictoris b, about 63 light-years away, has the mass of 10 Jupiters and a magnetic field thousands of times as strong as Earth’s.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A planet ten times Jupiter's mass, 63 light-years away, may be putting on an aurora display powered by a magnetic field thousands of times stronger than Earth's — and we caught the faintest whisper of it in radio waves. Somewhere out there, the sky is lit up in ways we can barely imagine.

discovery_articles.title: MRIs show brain changes linked to Alzheimer’s years in advance
discovery_articles.snippet: A thickening cortex, as shown in MRIs, preceded amyloid-beta accumulation, a known hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease, by up to seven years.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Long before the protein plaques of Alzheimer's appear, the brain's cortex quietly thickens — a change visible on MRI scans up to seven years in advance, like a structural warning no one knew to read. The disease, it turns out, announces itself far earlier than we thought.

discovery_articles.title: Ancient Rome’s Complicated Border
discovery_articles.snippet: What did Hadrian’s Wall actually do? Its history challenges the idea that walls simply separate one side from another.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Hadrian's Wall was less a hard border than a porous checkpoint — Romans and locals traded, mingled, and moved through it regularly, which complicates every tidy narrative about separation and control. Walls, it seems, have always been more complicated than the people who build them intend.

discovery_articles.title: How Virus-like ‘Jumping Genes’ Became Our Partners in Evolution
discovery_articles.snippet: Half of our genome is made of transposons — snips of DNA that can move and copy themselves. But they’re more than parasites or genetic junk. The post How Virus-like ‘Jumping Genes’ Became Our Partners in Evolution first appeared on Quanta Magazine
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Half of your DNA is made of ancient jumping genes — mobile snippets that once behaved like viruses and have since become deeply entangled with what makes us human. They're not junk; they've been quietly co-authoring us for millions of years.

discovery_articles.title: Lush Mixed-Media Collages by Clotilde Jiménez Piece Together an Artist’s Lineage
discovery_articles.snippet: Through vivid collages layering fragments of paper and fiber, Clotilde Jiménez echoes his own mélange of experiences and histories.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Clotilde Jiménez builds his collages from paper and fiber the way memory actually works — layered, fragmentary, never quite resolved into a single clean image. The lineage he's tracing isn't a family tree so much as a texture.

discovery_articles.title: Classical Musicians Interpret Astronauts’ Footage of the Planet for Earth Music Theater
discovery_articles.snippet: The multimedia project marries sonic experiences with incredible imagery captured from the International Space Station's orbit around Earth.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Classical musicians scored their compositions to footage of Earth captured from the ISS — and the result is less a nature documentary than a reckoning with scale, distance, and the strange intimacy of seeing home from outside it.

featured_read.title: On Not Being a Homeowner
featured_read.snippet: "Generational wealth shapes our futures and friendships, whether we talk about it or not."
featured_read.blurb: This essay sits quietly with the unspoken arithmetic of inheritance — how the gap between owning and renting quietly redrafts your relationships, your options, and your sense of belonging in the world. If you've ever smiled through a conversation about property ladders while feeling the floor shift beneath you, this one was written for you.

reading_room.title: Heather Cox Richardson has been awarded the inaugural Gitlin-Auster Defender of Democracy Award.
reading_room.snippet: Over the weekend, Writers for Democratic Action (WDA) awarded historian Heather Cox Richardson with its inaugural Gitlin-Auster Defender of Democracy Award, “established to honor a writer whose voice powerfully embodies the wisdom, courage, and steadfastness that marked the lives of
reading_room.blurb: Not an essay for this edition — this is an award announcement, and a brief one at that. No blurb generated.

reading_room.title: In Defense of Guilt by Association
reading_room.snippet: The wisdom of judging politicians by the company they keep
reading_room.blurb: Against the received wisdom that judging people by their associates is lazy thinking, this piece makes the uncomfortable case that it might actually be one of our sharper political tools — and that dismissing it flatters the wrong people.

reading_room.title: The Confrontation That Broke New York
reading_room.snippet: A new book sheds some light on the death of Jordan Neely and the trial that divided a post-pandemic city.
reading_room.blurb: The death of Jordan Neely and the trial that followed cracked New York open along fault lines that had been forming for years — this piece uses a new book to ask what a city owes its most vulnerable, and what we reveal about ourselves when the answer is contested in a courtroom.

reading_room.title: Sound guardians
reading_room.snippet: As Indonesia builds a new capital city, the race is on to preserve the sounds of the rainforest before they vanish forever - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: Before Indonesia's new capital city erases the rainforest that stood in its place, a small group of sound recordists is racing to archive what no photograph can capture — the living acoustic world of a forest in its last years. It's an elegy made of frequencies.

reading_room.title: Why it’s So Hard to Measure the Depth of the Ocean
reading_room.snippet: There are a lot of variables
reading_room.blurb: We've mapped the surface of Mars in finer detail than the floor of our own ocean — this piece dives into the surprisingly treacherous physics and politics of measuring a depth that refuses to hold still.
